questions.problem:
Consider the function $y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{2{e}^{{x}^{2}}g(x)}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡{({x}^{2}-2x-8)}^{2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-2x-8)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-2x-8)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x-2\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\cdot (2x-2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}(2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}(\frac{2x({x}^{2}-2x-8)-(4x-4)}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}(2x({x}^{2}-2x-8)-(4x-4)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}(2{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-16x-4x+4) \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-10x+2)}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)={x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-10x+2.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Notice that as $n\to 0,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{4/7n}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{1/n}=e
$$

Rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and applying our special limit, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{4/7n} & ={lim}_{n\to 0}{[{(1+n)}^{1/n}]}^{4/7} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{1/n}]}^{4/7} \\  & ={e}^{4/7} \\  & =\sqrt[7]{{e}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{3}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,(x){|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}x(\frac{3}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(({e}^{2})^{3})\,({e}^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{3})\,(1)]-3{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{6})-3x{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =6{e}^{2}-3({e}^{2}-1) \\  & =3({e}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the value of $a$ given that

$$
{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(\frac{1}{a+h}-\frac{1}{a})}{h}=-\frac{1}{4}\,.
$$

$a=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we let 

$$
L=\frac{(\frac{1}{a+h}-\frac{1}{a})}{h}=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Comparing this with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change,

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

we see that if we let $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$, we get

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(\frac{1}{a+h}-\frac{1}{a})}{h}=L.
$$

This confirms that $L={f}^{′}(a).$

Computing the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,{f}^{′}(a)=-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}},
$$

and so,  $L=-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}}.$

Finally, since $L=-\frac{1}{4},$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}} & =-\frac{1}{4} \\ {a}^{2} & =4 \\ a & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
On which of the following intervals can the extreme value theorem be applied to the function $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x?$    

I. $[0,\frac{\pi }{2}]$

II. $[0,\frac{\pi }{4})$

III. $[-\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}]$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the extreme value theorem is only applicable to closed intervals on which the function is continuous. 

With that in mind, let's take a look at each interval.

- The interval $[0,\frac{\pi }{2}]$  is closed, but the function is not defined at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Therefore, the extreme value theorem is not applicable.

- The interval $[0,\frac{\pi }{4})$ is not closed, so the extreme value theorem is not applicable.

- The interval $[-\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}]$ is closed, and the function is continuous on $[-\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4}].$ Therefore, the extreme value theorem is applicable.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "III only".
